mockText: 45 items in 50 minutes, with 4 hands-on items (logs, terminal, ordering, diagram), flags and a review screen. Cisco doesn't publish the real item count or the topic weights, so this is a stand-in that fits the real 50 minutes, with an even mix across the six domains.
lead: Cisco's entry-level networking cert. It proves you know how a network fits together and can troubleshoot the basics: addressing, cabling, Wi-Fi, switches and routers, and the commands a help desk tech runs every day. Cisco calls it the first step toward CCNA.
objSub: Six topic areas from Cisco's 100-150 exam topics. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: One 50-minute exam. Cisco doesn't publish a question count or a passing score; you get a pass/fail report when you finish. Test at a Pearson VUE center, online, or at a school's Certiport testing center.
cur.onote: Cisco numbers these topics but doesn't publish weights. The bars split study time about evenly across the six areas.

domains.name: Standards and Concepts
obj: Identify the building blocks of a network
TCP/IP and OSI models, frames and packets, addressing.
Tell bandwidth from throughput
Latency, delay, and speed tests vs iPerf.
Tell network types apart
LAN, WAN, MAN, CAN, PAN and WLAN, and common physical and logical topologies.
Compare cloud and on-premises
Public, private and hybrid cloud; SaaS, PaaS and IaaS; remote and hybrid work.
Describe common applications and protocols
TCP vs UDP, FTP, SFTP, TFTP, HTTP, HTTPS, DHCP, DNS, ICMP and NTP.

domains.name: Addressing and Subnet Formats
obj: Compare private and public addresses
Address classes and NAT.
Identify IPv4 addresses and subnets
Subnet masks, slash notation, subnet calculators and broadcast domains.
Identify IPv6 addresses
Address types and prefixes.

domains.name: Endpoints and Media Types
obj: Identify cables and connectors
Copper twisted pair, fiber and coax; RJ-45, RJ-11 and fiber connectors.
Compare Wi-Fi, cellular and wired links
Copper interference, fiber, 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands, licensed cellular, sources of interference.
Identify endpoint devices
IoT, computers, mobile devices, IP phones, printers and servers.
Set up and check connectivity on any OS
Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS: utilities, commands and Wi-Fi settings (SSID, authentication, WPA mode).

domains.name: Infrastructure
obj: Read Cisco status lights
Link light color and state, blinking or solid.
Cable devices from a diagram
Patch cables, switches and routers, small topologies, power and rack layout.
Identify device ports
Console, serial, fiber, Ethernet, SFP, USB and PoE.
Explain basic routing
Default gateways, Layer 2 vs Layer 3 switches, local vs remote networks.
Explain basic switching
MAC address tables, MAC filtering and VLANs.

domains.name: Diagnosing Problems
obj: Follow a troubleshooting method
Help desk policies, documentation, gathering information, prioritizing and tickets.
Capture packets with Wireshark
What a packet analyzer does; saving and opening .pcap files.
Run basic diagnostic commands
ping, ipconfig, ifconfig and ip, tracert and traceroute, nslookup, and how firewalls change the results.
Reach devices and collect data
RDP, SSH, Telnet, VPN, console, terminal emulators, management systems, cloud-managed networks (Meraki) and scripts.
Run basic Cisco show commands
show running-config, ip interface brief, ip route, version, mac address-table, cdp neighbors; privilege levels and help.

domains.name: Security
obj: Explain firewall filtering
Blocked ports and protocols; allow and deny rules.
Describe security basics
CIA, AAA, MFA, encryption, certificates, password rules, Active Directory, and threats like phishing, malware and DoS.
Secure a home or small-office Wi-Fi router
WPA, WPA2 and WPA3; Personal vs Enterprise.

extras.title: Address ranges to know
rows: Self-assigned when DHCP fails. A clue, not a fix.

extras.title: Help desk troubleshooting
rows: Gather information: what fails, since when, who else is affected.
Check the physical layer first: link lights, cables, Wi-Fi connection.
Check addressing: ipconfig or ip, then ping the gateway.
Check beyond the gateway: ping an outside IP, then test DNS with nslookup.
Fix one thing at a time and test after each change.
Document the cause, the fix and the result in the ticket.

method: Use the six areas above as your checklist. Cisco gives no weights, so cover all six.
Learn what each device and protocol does, and what it looks like when it breaks.
Build small networks in Packet Tracer and run ipconfig, ping, tracert and nslookup on your own PC until they're second nature.
Flashcards for private ranges, subnet masks, ports, cable types and show commands.
Timed 50-minute practice sets. Review every miss and why the other answers were wrong.
tips: 50 minutes goes fast. Cisco exams usually don't let you go back, so answer each question before you move on.
In command-output questions, the answer is often one field: the gateway, the mask or the status column.
Write the block sizes (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4) on your whiteboard before you start.
There's no penalty for guessing, so always pick something.

items: Price, time, languages and the link to the exam topics.
Russ White's book, the Cisco-approved self-study guide.
Free self-paced networking courses that follow the CCST topics.
Network simulator for cabling, switching and routing practice. Free with a Networking Academy account.
Beginner rooms on networking, the web and Linux.
Endless subnet questions until the math is automatic.
Capture your own traffic and open .pcap files.

quiz.q: A speed test on a user's laptop shows 940 Mbps to a nearby test server. Copying a large file to the file server at another site, over a 100 Mbps WAN link, runs at about 80 Mbps. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: The WAN link's 100 Mbps bandwidth is the limit, and 80 Mbps is the throughput actually achieved across it
Right. Bandwidth is the maximum a link can carry; throughput is what you really get after overhead and other traffic. The slowest link in the path sets the ceiling.
The laptop's network card is failing, because it should copy at 940 Mbps
The laptop tested fine locally. The copy crosses a 100 Mbps link, so it can never reach 940.
Throughput can only be lower than bandwidth when a cable is damaged
Throughput is always somewhat lower than bandwidth because of protocol overhead, latency and shared use.
The difference means DNS is slow
DNS only resolves the name at the start. It doesn't limit transfer speed.

quiz.q: Which pair of protocols normally runs over UDP?
o: DNS queries and TFTP
Right. Standard DNS lookups and TFTP both use UDP (ports 53 and 69). DNS falls back to TCP for large replies and zone transfers.
HTTPS and SSH
Both run over TCP (443 and 22).
FTP and SFTP
FTP uses TCP 20/21 and SFTP runs inside SSH on TCP 22.
HTTP and Telnet
Both use TCP (80 and 23).

quiz.q: A laptop shows IPv4 address 169.254.37.12, mask 255.255.0.0 and no default gateway. Other laptops on the same switch work fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: It couldn't get an address from a DHCP server
Right. 169.254.x.x (APIPA) is what Windows assigns itself when no DHCP offer arrives. Check the cable or port, then renew the lease.
The DNS server is down
A DNS outage breaks name lookups, but the laptop would still have a normal DHCP address and gateway.
The laptop's IP conflicts with another host
A conflict gives a duplicate-address warning on a normal address, not an APIPA address.
NAT on the router is misconfigured
NAT problems affect internet access. They don't stop a host from getting a local address.

quiz.q: A host is 192.168.40.77/26. What are its network and broadcast addresses?
o: Right. A /26 makes blocks of 64: .0, .64, .128, .192. Host .77 sits in the .64 block, which ends at .127.
That would be a /24. With a /26 the block is only 64 addresses wide.
.128 is the start of the next block, not the broadcast of this one.
Those are just the neighbors of .77. Subnets fall on block boundaries.

quiz.q: A PC 85 m from the switch works fine. A new 140 m run of Cat 6 copper to a guard shack shows no link at all. What is the BEST fix?
o: Use fiber for the run, or put a switch partway, because copper Ethernet is limited to 100 m
Right. Twisted-pair Ethernet is rated to 100 m per segment. Past that, use fiber or add a powered switch in between.
Swap the Cat 6 for Cat 5e
Cat 5e has the same 100 m limit, so it won't help.
Use a crossover cable
Modern ports detect cable type automatically (Auto-MDIX). Distance is the problem.
Turn on PoE on the switch port
PoE sends power. It doesn't extend the data distance.

quiz.q: A Windows laptop is on the right Wi-Fi network. ipconfig shows 10.20.5.33 with gateway 10.20.5.1. ping 10.20.5.1 works and ping 8.8.8.8 works, but ping www.example.com says it could not find the host. What should you check next?
o: The DNS server settings, using nslookup
Right. Reaching the gateway and an outside IP proves addressing and routing work. Failing only by name points to DNS.
The Wi-Fi password
A wrong password would stop the connection entirely, and pings to the gateway would fail.
The default gateway
The gateway answered and traffic reached 8.8.8.8, so the gateway is fine.
The Ethernet cable
It's on Wi-Fi, and the IP pings work, so the physical link is fine.

quiz.q: PC-A (192.168.1.10/24) and PC-B (192.168.2.10/24) plug into the same switch, both in VLAN 1. They can't ping each other. Why?
o: They're on different subnets, so traffic between them needs a router or Layer 3 switch
Right. Each PC sees the other as remote and sends to its default gateway. A plain Layer 2 switch can't route between subnets.
The switch's MAC address table is full
A full table makes the switch flood frames. It wouldn't stop these pings.
They need a crossover cable
Both connect to a switch with ordinary patch cables. Cabling isn't the issue.
DNS isn't configured
Pinging by IP address doesn't use DNS.

quiz.q: A switch receives a frame for a destination MAC address that isn't in its MAC address table. What does it do?
o: Floods the frame out every port in that VLAN except the one it arrived on
Right. Unknown unicast frames are flooded. When the destination replies, the switch learns its port.
Drops the frame
Switches flood unknown destinations instead of dropping them.
Sends the frame to the default gateway
Switches forward by MAC address within the VLAN. Default gateways are for hosts sending to other subnets.
Sends an ARP request to find the MAC
ARP is how hosts find a MAC for an IP. The switch doesn't ARP on a host's behalf.

quiz.q: Which Cisco command shows every interface with its IP address and up/down status in one short table?
o: show ip interface brief
Right. It's the quickest health check: interface, IP, method, status and protocol on one line each.
show running-config
It shows the whole configuration. Status isn't there, and it's long.
show version
It shows the software version, uptime and hardware, not per-interface status.
show mac address-table
It maps MAC addresses to switch ports. No IPs, no status.

quiz.q: A user calls and says “the internet is down.” Following a help desk method, what should you do FIRST?
o: Ask questions: what exactly fails, since when, and whether others are affected
Right. Gather information before you touch anything. Often the problem is one site, one app, or one user.
Reboot the core router
That would take everyone down to fix a problem you haven't confirmed.
Escalate to Tier 2 right away
Tier 2 expects the basics gathered first.
Replace the user's network cable
You don't know yet that it's physical. Fix after you've found the cause.

quiz.q: Which wireless security setting gives the STRONGEST protection for a small-office router when every device is modern?
o: WPA3-Personal
Right. WPA3 uses SAE, which resists offline password-guessing attacks better than WPA2's pre-shared key.
WEP
WEP was broken years ago and can be cracked in minutes.
WPA with TKIP
Original WPA and TKIP are deprecated and weak.
A hidden SSID with MAC filtering
Hidden SSIDs still show up in traffic and MAC addresses are easy to spoof. That's obscurity, not encryption.

quiz.q: A firewall's rule list ends with “deny any any.” A tech adds “permit tcp any host 10.1.1.20 eq 443” BELOW that line. What happens to HTTPS traffic to 10.1.1.20?
o: It's still blocked, because rules are checked top-down and the deny matches first
Right. Most firewalls and ACLs stop at the first match. The permit has to go above the deny.
It's allowed, because the more specific rule always wins
Rule order decides, not how specific the rule is.
It's allowed, because HTTPS is encrypted
Firewalls filter encrypted traffic by address and port the same as any other.
The firewall rejects the new rule as a duplicate
It's not a duplicate. It's accepted but never reached.

pbqs.title: Work the help desk queue
pbqs.scenario: Five tickets are waiting. For each one, pick the most likely cause and the best next step. Causes and steps can repeat.

rows.req: Laptop shows 169.254.10.4. Other users on the same switch are fine.
rows.why: APIPA means no DHCP offer arrived. Check the connection, then run ipconfig /release and /renew.

rows.req: PC can ping 8.8.8.8, but every browser says the server can't be found.
rows.why: Outside IPs answer, names don't. That's DNS: test with nslookup and check the DNS server setting.

rows.req: Static IP 10.5.5.20/24 with gateway 10.5.6.1. The user can print locally but can't reach anything off the subnet.
rows.why: 10.5.6.1 isn't in the 10.5.5.0/24 subnet, so the PC can't reach it. Set the gateway to the router's address in 10.5.5.0/24.

rows.req: Desk PC: no link light on the network card, and the switch shows the port as notconnect.
rows.why: No link on either end is physical. Reseat or swap the patch cable, then try another switch port.

rows.req: A user can open \\10.1.1.5\share by IP, but \\fileserver\share fails.
rows.why: By IP works, by name fails: the name isn't resolving. Check it with nslookup fileserver.

pbqs.title: Read the command output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a ticket. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
Interface   IP-Address  OK? Method Status                Protocol
Gi0/0       10.1.1.1    YES manual administratively down  down
items.why: “Administratively down” means someone ran shutdown on the interface. Enter the interface and run no shutdown.

items.log:
IPv4 Address. . . . : 169.254.88.3
Subnet Mask . . . . : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway . . :
items.why: A 169.254 address with no gateway is APIPA: the PC never got a DHCP lease.

items.log:
> intranet.example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address: 10.1.1.53
*** dns1.example.com can't find intranet.example.com: Non-existent domain
items.why: The DNS server answered, but has no record for that name. Check the spelling or add the record.

items.log:
1   <1 ms  <1 ms  <1 ms  10.1.1.1
2   10.1.1.1 reports: Destination net unreachable.
items.why: The gateway itself says it has no route to that network. The router needs a route (or a default route).

items.log:
GigabitEthernet1/0/5 is up, line protocol is up
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  4518 late collision, 2210 CRC
items.why: Half duplex with lots of late collisions and CRC errors is the classic duplex mismatch. Set both ends to auto, or both to the same fixed values.

items.log:
Vlan  Mac Address      Type     Ports
 30   0050.56aa.1b2c   DYNAMIC  Gi1/0/8
(Ticket: the printer on Gi1/0/8 belongs in VLAN 20, Printers)
items.why: The printer's MAC was learned in VLAN 30, so the port is assigned to the wrong VLAN. Move Gi1/0/8 to VLAN 20.

hereNote: The entry step on the Network path
mapSub: CCST Networking is the on-ramp to CCNA. Tap any cert to jump to it.

keep.text: A CCST earned on or after July 15, 2025 is valid for 5 years. One earned before that date doesn't expire.
keep.after: Renew by passing any current CCST, associate, professional or expert Cisco exam. Continuing education credits don't count for CCST, but passing CCNA renews it.

keep.text: CCST isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix. On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: For networking work roles, pair it with Network+ or CCNA, which are on the matrix.

keep.text: At $125 it's a cheap, quick proof that you know the fundamentals, and good practice for Cisco's exam style before CCNA.
keep.after: Add the Credly badge to your résumé and LinkedIn.
